lead: The hull, the deck and the rig are where a deposit goes. Walk round in a fixed order with the base's technician, sort what you find into what is fixed before you leave and what goes on the form, and only then sign.

sections.title: A fixed order, the technician beside you

qa.q: How do I record existing damage on a charter yacht at check-in?
qa.a: Write what it is, how big and where, take a wide and a close-up photo, and have the base's technician initial it on the **check-in form**. Notes you make alone are your word against the base's.

blocks.p: Start outside, from the quay: the hull from bow to stern on both sides, then the deck, then the rig. A fixed order is how nothing gets missed. Keep the technician with you: a mark goes on the form's boat outline with him present and initialling. Notes you make alone are your word against the base's on Friday.

fig.title: One mark, written properly
lines: What: gelcoat chip 3 cm, star cracks
Where: port bow, 40 cm aft of the stem
Photo 1: wide, to place it on the boat
Photo 2: close up, a coin for scale

blocks.p: Write what it is, how big and where. Star cracks mean an impact, so write cracks, not scratches: you sign for the boat as the form describes her, and 'general wear' describes nothing. Whatever happens before your signature goes on the form too. A gap noticed next morning is added, dated and initialled at the office before you sail.

blocks.rule: On Friday the signed form counts, not the technician's memory.

sections.title: From the quay, the dinghy and the bilge

qa.q: How can I tell if a charter yacht has run aground before?
qa.a: Look at the keel: **rusty keel bolts** or fresh paint at the keel joint are signs of a grounding. Ask for a keel check, because a keel scuff missing from the form becomes your grounding at check-out.

blocks.p: A keel scuff or a chipped rudder missing from the form at check-in becomes your grounding at check-out. If you do touch bottom during the week, check the bilge and keel bolts, photograph the keel and call the base the same day. Salt water in a locker only when heeled points to the deck joint: report that too.

sections.title: Fix it now or write it down

qa.q: What must the charter base fix before I leave, and what just goes on the form?
qa.a: Anything that can hurt someone or endanger the boat, such as a loose stanchion or a slipping winch, is **fixed before you leave**. What is worn but safe goes on the form with a photo.

blocks.p: Sort every finding into two piles. What can hurt someone or endanger the boat is **fixed by the base before you leave**: an entry on the form does not hold a guardrail. What is worn but safe is **written on the form** with a photo, so it stays the base's on Friday.

fig.note: Guardrail: all three fixed before you leave

blocks.p: The chain stopper, not the windlass, takes the anchor load. A winch's pawls stop the drum running back under load. Steering play that grows during the week, with a knock under the cockpit, is a cable or quadrant going: call the base and motor gently to the nearest harbour.

qa.q: Should a torn bimini be repaired at check-in or just noted on the form?
qa.a: Repaired: a tear, an open zip or a missing strap is fixed at check-in, because a **tear** grows in the first blow. A scratched window or a bent frame goes on the form.

blocks.p: At check-in a tear, an open zip or a missing strap is fixed, because a tear grows in the first blow; a scratched window and a bent frame go on the form.

sections.title: What you can check from the deck

qa.q: How do I check the mast and rigging when taking over a charter yacht?
qa.a: Sight up the mast from its foot for a straight mast and level spreaders, check the masthead with binoculars, and see each shroud's **turnbuckle** has a taped split pin. A broken strand or slack shroud is for the base's rigger.

fig.note: Sight up the mast; binoculars for the masthead

blocks.p: At the mast foot, sight up the groove: a straight mast, spreaders level with their end boots on, the deck flat round the foot. Binoculars from the quay show the masthead: wind vane and cups turning, antenna upright, light lenses whole. Each shroud ends in a **turnbuckle** with a split pin, so it cannot unwind, taped so sails and hands do not snag.

fig.title: Ask for the base's rigger
lines: Cap shroud slack on one side

blocks.p: None of these is a form entry or a job for you: the rigger puts it right before you sail, and the base gives you its backstay setting in writing. On the boom, a worn gooseneck pin is looked at now, and you ask for a line long enough to rig a preventer; a rigid kicker carries the boom without a topping lift. If strands break during the week, do not load the rig: call the base, and stay or motor back, sails down, as they decide.

sections.title: Two hulls and some parts of her own

qa.q: What extra should I check when chartering a catamaran?
qa.a: The inner hull faces and bridgedeck underside from the dinghy, that each wheel moves both rudders, both legs of the **forestay bridle**, the trampoline lacing, the davit welds, and that the saloon door locks.
